i think it's worse than this. If you come looking to learn D3, you get a website that has nice examples and a few tutorials, that are not maintained and typically refer to older versions. There are several documents explaining version changes, and then you get passed to Observable when you start looking for more up to date examples. 

 And, honestly, it has all the same issues - inconsistent documentation, multiple versions, and of course the variant framework of Observable.  And if you consider embedding Observables as the base toolset, you will face this startling admission on Embedding an Observable : 

> along the way, our documentation and support has grown haphazardly, through responses to forum posts, leaving behind a trail of examples and warnings you have to stumble upon and bookmark for later. Many of those problems remain unsolved, but we are either working to fix them or working to document the workarounds that have been floating around the community, and collect them in places you are more likely to see them.  
(quoting https://observablehq.com/@observablehq/embeds ) 

 No doubt there is enthusiastic technical innovation going on but it's remarkably difficult to find a current set of best practice examples and sound tutorials to scaffold learning for those who don't already know where the version issues and workarounds actually are.

body:
D3 itself has **no built-in sanitization** - it is a data transformation + DOM-binding library, not a security framework. The injection risk depends entirely on which D3 API you use:

| API | Under the hood | Safe? |
|-----|---------------|-------|
| `.text(value)` | `element.textContent = value` | Yes - always treated as text |
| `.attr('class', value)` | `element.setAttribute(...)` | Yes for most attributes |
| `.html(value)` | DOM tree mutation via parsed HTML | **No** - executes embedded scripts in some contexts |
| `.attr('href', value)` | `element.setAttribute('href', ...)` | Risky if value starts with `javascript:` |
| `.on('click', fn)` | `addEventListener` | Yes - takes a function, not a string |

**The main risk: `.html()`**

D3's `.html()` method parses its argument as HTML markup and injects the resulting DOM tree, which can include script elements and event handler attributes. Avoid it when the value comes from user or external data:

```js
// DANGEROUS if `d` comes from untrusted data:
svg.selectAll('text').data(data).join('text').html(d => d.label);

// SAFE: use .text() for plain string content:
svg.selectAll('text').data(data).join('text').text(d => d.label);
```

**SVG `<foreignObject>`** can embed arbitrary HTML - apply the same care.

**Practical rules:**
1. Prefer `.text()` over `.html()` everywhere possible
2. If you must call `.html()` with external data, sanitize first with [DOMPurify](https://github.com/cure53/DOMPurify): `selection.html(DOMPurify.sanitize(d.label))`
3. Validate `href`/`src` attribute values against an allowlist of protocols (`https:`, relative paths)
4. CSP headers (`script-src 'self'`) are your last line of defense and block inline script injection even if sanitization is missed

D3 visualizations driven by fully controlled/static data have no injection risk. The risk surface is purely at the point where untrusted data enters a DOM-mutating D3 call.

body: The outerRadius can be [specified](https://github.com/d3/d3-shape#arc_outerRadius) either as a constant or as a function of the datum, and the code normalizes constant values to a function. If we wanted to change that, then the API would return inconsistently either a function or a constant—and this would put the burden on any client code to check whether it's a function or a number, possibly retransforming the constant to a function. (Also, it would be backwards-compatible.)
